items.title: Apple accelerates Mac Mini and Mac Studio launch due to unexpected enterprise AI demand amid global memory shortages [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Apple caught off guard by AI demand for Mac Mini and Mac Studio
items.summary:
Apple's early announcement of new Mac Mini and Mac Studio models was driven by stronger-than-expected enterprise demand for AI hardware, according to The Information. The company typically releases new Macs in autumn, but the surge in AI-related sales prompted an unusually early launch just before new iPhone models are expected. Apple emphasized features like linking multiple Mac Studios for large AI model workloads, targeting business and developer customers rather than consumers.

Despite this demand, Apple was reportedly unprepared with no dedicated engineering team for business customers or a clear enterprise AI strategy. The company declined requests from businesses seeking access to its Private Cloud Compute infrastructure and is instead relying on partners like WebAI and Mount Thor for AI tools on Apple hardware. The global memory shortage has also caused many Mac Mini and Mac Studio configurations to be out of stock for months, leading some enterprise customers to consider alternative hardware such as Nvidia's DGX Spark.

items.originalTitle: Wafer, An Inference Provider That Uses Non-Nvidia Chips, Lands Acquisition Offers and $200 Million-Plus Valuation
items.summary: Wafer, a San Francisco-based startup founded in May 2025, has raised $40 million in a Series A funding round co-led by Marathon Management Partners and Chemistry VC, reaching a valuation above $200 million. The company provides AI inference services that optimize open-source models for various AI workloads using chips other than Nvidia's. Wafer's AI inference engineers tailor optimizations based on specific use cases, such as voice-based agents requiring rapid prompt handling versus coding agents needing longer context retention.

items.originalSummary:
Developers and chip designers are increasingly upbeat about the benefits of using AI to supercharge the process of designing and optimizing AI chips, as my colleague Phoebe wrote about last week.

Now, a year-old inference provider, Wafer, is trying a similar approach: using AI to improve the way models run on a variety of chips and then helping businesses to run those models.

The San Francisco-based startup recently raised $40 million in Series A funding co-led by Marathon Management Partners and Chemistry VC, cofounder and CEO Emilio Andere told The Information exclusively. The startup’s valuation now stands above $200 million, according to a person with knowledge of the round. Andere, who cofounded Wafer with his college best friend Steven Arellano in May 2025, declined to comment on the valuation.

Andere said Wafer has developed AI agents—which it calls AI inference engineers—that can take a business’ specific AI workload and optimize open-source models for that workload. For instance, Wafer’s AI inference engineers would make different optimizations to an open-source model for a voice-based AI agent, which needs to be able to quickly handle repeated prompts and bursts of traffic, than they would for a coding agent, which needs to be able to remember important context over longer periods of time, Andere said.

items.originalTitle: AIR raises $50M to help companies vet the skills and add-ons AI agents use
items.summary:
AIR, an AI security startup founded by former Israeli intelligence officers, has raised $50 million to develop a platform that identifies AI agents running within companies and continuously vets the skills, plugins, and add-ons they use. The platform blocks unauthorized or risky components and maintains a whitelist by monitoring changes and potential malicious behavior in real time.

The company has over 20 customers, including large enterprises in regulated industries like financial services and pharmaceuticals. AIR aims to address the emerging software supply chain risks posed by AI agents operating autonomously across enterprise systems, offering visibility and enforcement tools to prevent attackers from exploiting AI agent components. The startup faces competition from other security firms but emphasizes its continuous vetting approach as a key differentiator.

items.summary:
Tarn Adams, creator of Dwarf Fortress, criticized the gaming industry's current state during Gamescom 2026, attributing turmoil to generative AI adoption and widespread layoffs. He expressed concern that CEOs expect AI to replace human developers, leading to unstable business models and management issues.

Adams highlighted that this problem extends beyond gaming, citing examples of layoffs caused by misunderstandings of technical roles and the overreliance on AI-generated outputs. He warned that without changes, the industry may face repeated cycles of disruption and reckoning driven by unrealistic expectations of AI capabilities.

The service integrates with email, calendar, and messaging apps to provide daily checklists and proactive reminders, aiming to reduce the mental load on parents.

Founded by former tech executives, Fambot uses multiple AI models without training on user data and offers interaction via text, web, and mobile apps. Tested by over 1,000 families, the startup plans to expand integrations with school and sports apps and expects to charge a subscription fee similar to Netflix after its current free beta phase.

Google has introduced Google Pics, a new suite of AI-driven creative design tools for Workspace users aimed at simplifying the creation and editing of professional-grade images. Built on the Gemini and Nano Banana generative AI models, Google Pics offers precise prompt-based image manipulation, including object and text editing, and supports upscaling to 2K or 4K resolutions. The tool is available as a standalone app and integrates with Google Docs and Slides, with plans to extend to Drive soon.

Google designed Pics to address challenges businesses face with AI image generation, such as inconsistent results and complex workflows, enabling teams to create marketing materials, presentations, and product visuals without needing advanced graphic design skills. The service is rolling out to Workspace users on Business Standard, Business Plus, Enterprise Standard, Enterprise Plus, Google AI Pro and Ultra personal plans, and Google AI Pro for Education plans.

items.originalTitle: Introducing wrapture
items.summary:
Introducing wrapture

New from Graham Dumpleton (of wrapt, mod_wsgi, and New Relic's Python agent fame), who describes Wrapture as taking the monkeypatching ideas from wrapt and extending them to apply to testing and tracing at the same time.

Wrapture (full documentation here) makes it easy to wrap any function or method such that all access can be traced, or can be overridden to return a different value.

It acts as both an alternative to unittest.mock and a way to implement tracing against an existing project:

Attaching observation to code you do not control, recording what flows through it, and doing so without disturbing the program being watched, is a problem I have never really stopped thinking about.

Wrapture includes OpenTelemetry support and even has an entirely configuration-based mechanism for adding tracing to an existing Python project, which looks like this:

capture = "summary" [[observe]] target = "domain:Calculator" name = ["outer", "inner"] [[sink]] type = "jsonlines" path = "trace.jsonl"

This is still a very young project - just a few weeks old - but it's off to a very promising start.

Interestingly, this is also Graham's first attempt at large entirely agent-driven project:

Every line of code and documentation in wrapture was written by an AI assistant working under my direction. I want to be upfront about that, and equally upfront about what it was not. This was not vibe coding, where a one-shot prompt produces a pile of generated code and the person driving hopes for the best because they lack the knowledge to judge what came back. Vibe coding has earned its bad reputation. I engineered wrapture carefully from the start. I have spent a long time in this particular corner of Python and knew exactly what the result needed to be, and the AI was the means of producing it rather than the source of the design.

In a follow-up post, Unit testing with wrapture, Graham shows the testing patterns supported by the new library:

def test_stub_with_wrapture(): with wrapture.binding( Gateway, "charge" ).on_call.returns({ "id": "stub", "amount": 0} ): assert OrderService().place( 500 )["id"] == "stub"

And this neat example of a test that calls and then modifies the return value from the original method:

def test_pinned_result_with_wrapture(): charge = wrapture.binding( Gateway, "charge" ) charge.on_call.transforms_result( lambda r: {**r, "id": "ch_TEST"} ) with charge: assert OrderService().place( 500 ) == { "id": "ch_TEST", "amount": 500 }

(In both of these examples the OrderService().place(...) method calls Gateway().charge(...).)

items.title: Reframe Raises Funds to Bring Amazon Robotics Know-How to Home Building [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Reframe Raises Funds to Bring Amazon Robotics Know-How to Home Building
items.summary:
For all the talk of robots that look like humans, the next robots to move into people’s houses could look more like ducks. Sales of such a robot, made by open-source model platform Hugging Face, reached more than $2.5 million on its first day on Thursday.

Microduck, which costs $399, waddles around on two tiny legs and cocks its Wall-E-like head to inspect its surroundings. It could fulfill my prediction from January that the most successful home robot of the year will not be a full-blown humanoid, but a more humble robot designed for a single purpose. In this case, that purpose is mostly being really cute. 

One person who is sure to appreciate the cute factor is Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia, which has agreed to buy Hugging Face for $12.9 billion, my colleagues reported last week. Huang has made clear his fondness for robots, which he sees as the next frontier for AI after language models, and has brought Disney’s droids on stage during his keynotes. 

The robot’s software (but not its hardware design) is open-source, which Nvidia is championing in its in-house efforts as well as acquisitions like Hugging Face. It learns new skills, such as roller skating or kicking a mini soccer ball, using reinforcement learning in computer simulations—a perfect application for Nvidia’s AI chips.

Meanwhile, 1X Technologies, which received over 10,000 pre-orders for its home humanoids in October, still has not delivered any to customers. SoftBank is now in talks to buy a majority stake in 1X, my colleagues and I reported last week.

Meanwhile . . .

One April morning, Jonathan Talbot drove to the lot in Altadena, Calif., where he was rebuilding after his home was destroyed in last year's Eaton Fire. A crane lifted pre-built pieces of a new house from three trucks that had hauled them across the country. A piece of drywall had cracked in transit, and some closet shelves had fallen, but these were easy enough to fix. By the afternoon, the house was standing. “It was a very emotional day,” said Talbot, who is a product manager at Warner Bros. Discovery.

When Talbot receives the keys in the next month or two, he’ll become one of the first owners of a house built by Reframe Systems, which uses industrial robot arms to make modular homes in a factory before shipping and assembling them. The four-year old Massachusetts-based startup raised $40 million in a Series A extension funding round that closed a month ago, co-founder and CEO Vikas Enti told The Information exclusively.
